title: Why Some Wrecks Survive
description: Shipworms, brackish seas, oxygen-free depths and mud: what turns a wreck into a time capsule

concepts.title: A Moment Frozen in Time
concepts.contentHtml:
Most archaeological sites build up slowly. A city mound holds centuries of rubbish, rebuilding and reuse, and an archaeologist has to tease apart which objects ever belonged together. A shipwreck is different. It is often a closed find: an assemblage that went down in minutes, with everything aboard in use on the same day. The cargo, the cooking pots, the sailors' gaming pieces and the ship itself are fixed at one moment. That is why the Late Bronze Age ship found at Uluburun, in Turkey, is described as an undisturbed time capsule of the past.

There is a catch, and it explains most of this topic. The sea is also very good at destroying things. Wood is eaten, iron rusts, currents scatter what is left, and people salvage whatever they can reach. Even the dead usually vanish. Unless they are covered by sediment or protected in some other way, the bodies of shipwreck victims are normally swept away to decay or be eaten by fish.1 Complete skeletons have come from the Mary Rose, which sank in 1545, and the Vasa, which sank in 1628, and both ships settled into mud close to port.

So the real question behind every famous wreck is not only what sank, but why any of it survived. The answer usually comes down to three enemies of preservation:

  • Borers: animals that tunnel into wood, above all the shipworm.
  • Oxygen, which those animals and most decay organisms need.
  • Movement: tides, currents and storms that break a hull apart and spread it across the seabed.

Take away the borers, the oxygen or the movement, and a wreck can last for thousands of years. The next two concepts show each of these at work, from the brackish Baltic to the oxygen-free depths of the Black Sea. Keep the three in mind: every wreck in the lessons that follow survived, or failed to, because of them.

concepts.title: The Clam That Eats Ships
concepts.contentHtml:
The worst enemy of a wooden wreck is not a worm at all. The shipworm is a bivalve, a mollusc in the same group as clams and mussels, with a long soft body and two small, finely serrated shells at its front end. Its larvae drift in the plankton for about 14 days and, at roughly a quarter of a millimetre long, settle on any wood they meet. Once a larva becomes an adult it never leaves. Repeated rasping of its shells cuts a perfectly circular tunnel, and bacteria living inside it, Teredinibacter turnerae, help it digest the wood. In salty Scandinavian seas such borers can destroy exposed timber within years or even months.

Now look at the Baltic Sea. It is brackish, only partly salty, and that is its great gift to archaeology. So far its salinity has been too low for shipworms to spread through it. One estimate puts the number of wrecks in the Baltic at around 100,000, at least 6,000 of them of high archaeological importance.1 The Vasa in Stockholm is the best-known example of what this water can keep.

Is the archive safe? Shipworm outbreaks have struck Danish waters and the southern Baltic repeatedly over the past hundred years, and in the 2000s there were signs that Teredo navalis, the only shipworm species known in the Baltic, might push further in, possibly helped by climate change. An EU project, WRECKPROTECT, modelled salinity, temperature, oxygen and currents to predict where attacks were most likely. It found no evidence of a further spread; the currents tend to carry larvae out of the Baltic rather than deeper in. A 2018 study at the University of Rostock likewise found no current spread to the east, into the Baltic's less salty waters. For now, the clam that eats ships is held at the door.

concepts.title: Mud, Darkness and No Oxygen
concepts.contentHtml:
Shipworms need oxygen, and that is their weak point. The Mary Rose shows it beautifully. When Henry VIII's warship sank in 1545 she came to rest on her starboard side, and silt, sand and seaweed flowed in through her open gunports until the hull was full. The starboard side lay buried under a blanket of organic-rich silt that cut off the oxygen, so shipworm and gribble could not live there.1 Conditions like these, with no free oxygen, are called anaerobic. The port side stuck up into open water. Gribble and shipworm riddled it, tides and currents wore it down, and eventually it collapsed. When the wreck was rediscovered in the 1970s, only four timbers were protruding from the seabed. What was raised in 1982 is, in effect, the half of a ship that the mud protected.

The same rule holds in most salty seas: the parts of wooden wrecks that survive are those buried in sediment, where there is too little oxygen for borers. Burial is partly luck. A ship that lands on soft mud may be swallowed; one that lands on bare rock stays exposed.

The Black Sea takes the principle to an extreme. It has only a narrow connection to the Mediterranean, so fresh river water floats on top of salty Mediterranean water and the two layers barely mix. Below about 150 metres there is almost no oxygen, and wood-eating animals cannot survive. Water like this is called anoxic, and ancient ships that sink into it can stay intact for thousands of years, masts and all.

Antarctica offers a third kind of refuge. When Shackleton's Endurance was filmed 3,008 metres down in 2022, a deep-sea biologist suggested that the wood-munching animals of other oceans are simply absent from the forest-free Antarctic. You will return to both of these deep wrecks in lesson 6.

title: Antikythera: Sponge Divers and the First Salvage
description: Easter 1900, a storm, a bronze arm, the salvage that began underwater archaeology, and the return

concepts.title: A Storm, a Diver and a Bronze Arm
concepts.contentHtml:
Around Easter 1900, two boats of sponge fishermen from the island of Syme, in the Dodecanese, were driven by bad weather to anchor off Antikythera, a rocky island between Kythera and Crete. The channel there was one of the main shipping routes between the eastern and western Mediterranean in antiquity, and a dangerous one, with sudden currents. When the weather improved, one of the divers went down hoping to find sponges. At a depth of about 50 metres, some 25 metres from the shore, he found an ancient wreck instead, and he came back up holding the arm of a bronze statue.1

What lay below was the cargo of a big merchant ship, a freighter of about 300 tons, that had sunk around 70–50 BCE. The objects aboard ranged in date from the 4th to the 1st century BCE:

  • bronze and marble statues and statuettes;
  • at least 23 amphorae from Rhodes, Kos, Ephesos and the Adriatic coast;
  • fine plates and cups, gold jewellery, and luxury glass and silver vessels;
  • bronze fittings from furniture and wooden parts of the ship itself.

In all, 378 ancient works of art and coins came up. The ship carried luxury goods from the eastern Mediterranean, probably for wealthy buyers in Rome, at a time when Greek art was flowing west to Italy.

Among the finds was a corroded lump of bronze that nobody noticed for about eight months: the fragments of the Antikythera mechanism, the geared astronomical calculator explored in other topics in this app. Here the point is the site. The mechanism exists today only because one ship sank with it in the right place, and that wreck was about to become the first ancient shipwreck ever investigated by archaeologists.

concepts.title: Ten Months That Cost a Life
concepts.contentHtml:
The Greek government decided to recover the cargo, with the help of three ships of the Greek Royal Navy. What followed has been called the investigation that inaugurated underwater archaeology, but it looked nothing like a modern excavation. The diving was done by the same sponge fishermen who had found the wreck, and 50 metres is a dangerous depth to work at day after day. Conditions were harsh. The operation lasted ten months, until the end of September 1901, and by then one diver had died and two had been permanently disabled.1

The salvors raised what they could see and lift. The oldest find is the bronze Antikythera Youth, which came up in five fragments, and putting it back together became a saga of its own. The Greek sculptor Kaloudis made a first restoration in 1901. In 1902 the French sculptor André rejoined the pieces with metal plates, with only partial success. The statue was taken apart again in 1948 and reassembled by specialists in work that ran into 1953. Another celebrated find was the bronze head of an elderly, bearded man with inlaid eyes, known as the Philosopher.

What could a salvage like this not keep? By 1901 the divers had recovered every artefact visible on the seabed. But the value of a wreck lies as much in where things lie as in what they are. The position of each object, relative to the hull and to everything else, is what lets archaeologists work out how a ship was loaded, who was aboard and how it broke up. Lift objects without recording that, and the information is gone for good.

So Antikythera is both a triumph and a warning. It filled galleries of the National Archaeological Museum in Athens and gave the world its most famous ancient machine. It also shows what happens when a wreck is treated as a mine rather than a site: you keep the treasures and lose the story. The rest of this topic is, in a sense, the long effort to keep both.

concepts.title: Going Back: Bones Under the Sherds
concepts.contentHtml:
The story did not end in 1901. Jacques Cousteau's team dived on the wreck in 1976 and found scattered human bones; the osteoarchaeologist Argyro Nafplioti later concluded that they came from at least four people, including a young man, a woman and a teenager. In 2014 a new team co-directed by Brendan Foley of the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, with expert technical divers and members of the Greek archaeological service, relocated and mapped the 50-metre-deep site and began to excavate. Their bet was that much of the cargo still lay buried in the sediment, out of the salvors' reach. They found wine jars, glassware, two bronze spears from statues, gold jewellery, the crew's table jugs, enormous anchors, and a teardrop-shaped lead weight that may be the first known example of a war dolphin, a defensive weapon that ancient texts say merchant ships carried to smash hostile vessels.

On 31 August 2016 the divers uncovered a human skeleton under about half a metre of pottery sherds and sand:1 part of a skull with three teeth, two arm bones, pieces of rib and two femurs, apparently from one person, stained amber-red by corroded iron objects around them. The team nicknamed the person Pamphilos, after a name scratched on a wine cup from the wreck. The ancient-DNA specialist Hannes Schroeder was delighted to find both petrous bones, the dense bones behind the ear that preserve DNA better than any other part of the skeleton. Any analysis needed permission from the Greek authorities.

Why so many people on one ancient wreck, when most yield none? Partly because few wrecks have been searched so thoroughly. Foley also reads it as a clue to how the ship died: a vessel perhaps more than 40 metres long, with several decks, smashed against the island's cliffs by a storm so violently that people were trapped below. That is an interpretation, not a certainty, but notice where it comes from: where things and people lie, exactly what the first salvage could not record.

title: Bass at Gelidonya: Archaeology Goes Underwater
description: Cape Gelidonya in 1960, the first seabed excavation to land standards, and the tools that followed

concepts.title: Six Lessons at the YMCA
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1954 Kemal Aras, a sponge diver from Bodrum in Turkey, stumbled on a heap of ancient cargo 26 to 28 metres deep off Cape Gelidonya, on Turkey's southern coast. He described it to Peter Throckmorton, an American journalist and amateur archaeologist who was cataloguing ancient wrecks along the coast. Throckmorton relocated the site in 1959, recognised that it was very old, and asked the University Museum of the University of Pennsylvania to organise an excavation.

The man chosen to direct it was a surprise. George Bass had just begun doctoral studies in classical archaeology, and his department chairman asked whether he would learn to dive. He took only six diving lessons at a local YMCA before leaving for Turkey.1 His first open-water dive, in 1960, was in the Bosphorus with Claude Duthuit, who became the chief diver of the team that would later grow into the Institute of Nautical Archaeology (INA).

That summer the team camped on a narrow beach, sheltered their machine shop under a torn parachute scrounged from a US Air Force base, and dived from two sponge boats. The result was three firsts. In 1960 Gelidonya became the first shipwreck excavation carried out to completion on the seabed, the first conducted to the standards of an excavation on land, and the first directed by an archaeologist who dived himself.2 At Antikythera the people underwater had been sponge fishermen; at Gelidonya the person responsible for the record was on the seabed.

That is the real revolution. Underwater archaeology is not diving for antiquities; it is applying the same discipline of excavation, recording and publication that archaeologists use on land, in a place where every minute of work is rationed by air and depth. After the excavation, with the Turkish government's permission, Bass started a museum of underwater archaeology in Bodrum Castle, and objects from Gelidonya are displayed in Bodrum to this day.

concepts.title: What a Small Ship Said
concepts.contentHtml:
Around 1200 BCE a small merchant ship apparently ripped its bottom open on a rock pinnacle off Gelidonya. It sank slowly, spilling objects in a line, and settled with its stern on a large boulder. Most of its cargo was the makings of bronze: copper ingots, the white remains of tin ingots, and scrap bronze tools from Cyprus that were meant to be melted down and recast. Stone hammerheads, polishers, a whetstone and a large flat stone that may have served as an anvil suggest that a metalworker, a travelling tinker, sailed with the cargo.

Even the hull had something to say. Its planks were held together with pegged mortise-and-tenon joints, the method later used in Greek and Roman ships, and the brushwood laid under the cargo as padding gave, for the first time, a practical meaning to the brushwood Odysseus puts in the boat he builds in the Odyssey.

Then the hard question: whose ship was it? The excavators looked at the crew's own belongings rather than the cargo, since cargo is made to travel. Scarabs and a scarab-shaped plaque seem to have been made on the Syro-Palestinian coast rather than in Egypt, the stone mortars were of Syro-Palestinian type, and a Syrian cylinder seal looked like the merchant's own signature. The excavators concluded that the ship was probably Canaanite or early Phoenician, though it might have been Cypriot, because so many Near Eastern objects turn up on Cyprus in this period.1 Notice the hedge: national labels for Bronze Age ships are inferences, not certainties.

A site is never quite finished, either. Return visits in the late 1980s, nearly thirty years after the excavation, found two well-preserved Mycenaean stirrup jars about 50 metres from the main wreckage, Greek pots on a probably Levantine ship. Uluburun, in the next lesson, would test these ideas with a far richer cargo.

concepts.title: From Grids to Point Clouds
concepts.contentHtml:
Working on the seabed changes every part of an excavation. At Gelidonya the divers went down twice a day, for forty minutes in the morning and twenty-eight in the afternoon, decompressing at the end of each dive. An early underwater metal detector traced a trail of artefacts about a hundred metres long, which is how the team knew the ship had sunk slowly after hitting the rock. Cargo had fused into hard lumps of concretion, so divers lifted them whole with an air-filled balloon and fitted them together on land like a giant jigsaw. Cleaned, they revealed copper ingots still stacked as they had been in the hold 3,200 years earlier.

Through the 1960s the team refined these methods on Byzantine wrecks at Yassıada, in Turkey, where many techniques now considered standard were worked out. By the time the Mary Rose was excavated between 1979 and 1982, the toolkit looked recognisably modern. Side-scan sonar and sub-bottom profiling had found a strange W-shaped feature beneath the seabed. Divers worked with hands, trowels, paintbrushes and airlifts, suction pipes that waft silt away down-tide. A grid of bright yellow pipe divided the site into small areas matching the ship's decks and main beams, and every artefact and timber was recorded on a uniquely numbered dive log.1 More than 500 volunteer divers took part.

Deeper water needs robots. ROVs (remotely operated vehicles) carry cameras, lights and lasers to depths no diver can reach, and photogrammetry, a method that uses overlapping 2D photographs to create 3D images, turns thousands of pictures into a measured model. In the Black Sea, a team used two ROVs to photograph wrecks and build 3D models of them without disturbing them at all.

That last phrase marks the biggest change since 1960. Recording has become so good that, for many archaeologists, leaving a wreck where it lies and documenting it is the preferred option. You will see that principle written into international law in lesson 7.

title: Uluburun: A Bronze Age Cargo
description: Ten tonnes of copper, a tonne of tin, glass, ivory and a gold scarab: trade around 1300 BCE

concepts.title: Metal Biscuits with Ears
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1982 a Turkish sponge diver working near Kaş, on Turkey's south-west coast, described seeing metal biscuits with ears on the seabed off the cape of Uluburun. The description was soon recognised: oxhide ingots, flat copper slabs named for their resemblance to a stretched ox hide, whose projecting corners were the ears. They were a standard form for shipping Late Bronze Age metal. The find proved to be an elite shipment, a cargo of the kind of exotic and valuable goods that kings and wealthy merchants exchanged.

Excavating it was gruelling. The wreck lies 44 to 61 metres deep on a steep slope, where its cargo had spilled over some 250 square metres, and at that depth each dive is short. The Institute of Nautical Archaeology excavated it over 11 seasons between 1984 and 1994, logging more than 22,000 dives and raising about 17 tonnes of artefacts.1 The depth was also the wreck's protection: it had never been plundered.

When did it sink? Radiocarbon dates and recognisable pottery types place the wreck in the late 14th century BCE. INA dates it to about 1320 BCE, give or take 15 years, and other estimates put it between 1330 and 1300 BCE. One object adds a neat check. A unique gold scarab aboard names Nefertiti, the wife of the pharaoh Akhenaten, who reigned from about 1352 to 1336 BCE. An object like that gives a date after which the ship must have sunk, because it cannot have gone down before the scarab was made; archaeologists call this a terminus post quem.

Only a little of the hull survived, but enough to reconstruct a ship about 15 metres long and 5 metres wide, able to carry up to 20 tonnes of cargo. It was built of Lebanese cedar, wood prized in antiquity, with pegged mortise-and-tenon joints, the same technique seen at Gelidonya, and had a proto-keel rather than a true keel. Few finds come closer to a full inventory of a Bronze Age voyage.

concepts.title: Reading the Hold
concepts.contentHtml:
The bulk cargo was raw material for bronze. INA counts 354 copper ingots of the oxhide type, alongside smaller bun-shaped ingots; together the copper weighed about ten tonnes. About a tonne of tin came with it. The Uluburun ship was carrying copper and tin in the usual ratio of 10:1 for making bronze.1 Counts differ between publications: one widely read summary gives 348 copper ingots in all, a reminder to check the numbers in secondary sources against the excavators' own.

Around the metal was packed a whole economy:

  • Glass: perhaps more than 175 disc-shaped ingots in dark blue, turquoise, purple and yellow, probably cheaper stand-ins for lapis lazuli, turquoise, amethyst and amber.
  • Resin: at least 149 Canaanite jars, most of them filled with terebinth resin.
  • Exotics: ebony logs, an elephant tusk, 14 hippopotamus teeth, ostrich eggshells, Baltic amber, an Italian sword and Mesopotamian cylinder seals.
  • Luxuries: gold and silver jewellery, carved ivory containers, and the gold scarab of Nefertiti.

Who was aboard? Weapons, galley wares, balance weights and lutes with tortoise-shell sound boxes point to a Syro-Canaanite crew. Four sets of balances suggest four merchants, and Mycenaean seals and personal effects suggest at least two passengers from the Greek mainland. The ship was probably sailing west, perhaps from a Levantine port such as Tell Abu Hawam, near modern Haifa.

Was this commerce or diplomacy? The mix of goods closely resembles inventories of gifts exchanged between the rulers of Egypt and western Asia, so it may have been a royal shipment. Yet the four sets of balances, and the scrap gold and silver kept for payments, look like the tools of merchants. INA itself describes the cargo as fit for kings, heads of state or wealthy merchants, and the evidence does not force a choice. Either way, the hold of one small ship drew on Africa, the Levant, Cyprus, the Aegean, Mesopotamia and the Baltic.

concepts.title: Where Did the Tin Come From?
concepts.contentHtml:
Copper was the easy part: lead isotope analysis tied the Uluburun copper to Cyprus. Tin is the great puzzle of the Bronze Age. Bronze needed it, yet where the Mediterranean's tin was mined is still not resolved. In the 1990s a lead isotope study by Aslıhan Yener and colleagues suggested two sources for the Uluburun tin: the Kestel mine in Turkey's Taurus Mountains and some unidentified place in Central Asia.

In 2022 a team including Wayne Powell and Michael Frachetti analysed 105 of the tin ingots, roughly 90 percent of the tin on board, using tin isotopes, and published a striking answer in Science Advances. About one-third of the tin, they concluded, came from the Mušiston mine in Central Asia, more than 2,000 miles from Haifa, and two-thirds from Kestel.1 If right, small communities of highland herders in Central Asia were supplying metal to Mediterranean markets.

In 2023 four specialists, Daniel Berger, Kai Kaniuth, Gerhard Brügmann and Ernst Pernicka, replied in Frontiers in Earth Science that the arguments do not support such far-reaching conclusions. Tin isotope values vary widely within a deposit and overlap heavily between deposits, so tin isotopes alone never give an unambiguous answer.2 The 2022 study's dating of the ores, they argued, rested on a single lead isotope ratio. Instead they matched part of the cargo to Late and Middle Bronze Age tin ingots found off Israel and in Britain, proposed south-west England as a very likely source, and allowed that other ingots might come from Afghanistan or elsewhere.

So the question is open, and it is a lesson in how provenance science works. A chemical fingerprint is only as good as the reference data for every possible source, and two careful teams can read the same measurements differently. What both readings share is the scale: some of the tin on one small ship had travelled thousands of kilometres before it ever reached the sea.

title: Vasa and Mary Rose: Raising Warships
description: Why Sweden's Vasa and Henry VIII's Mary Rose sank, how they were raised, and the decades of drying

concepts.title: Vasa: 1,300 Metres and No Farther
concepts.contentHtml:
In January 1625 Sweden's king, Gustav II Adolf, contracted the Dutch master shipwright Henrik Hybertsson to build four new ships. One of them, Vasa, was to be the most powerful warship in the Baltic. Hybertsson fell ill and handed over to his assistant, Hein Jakobsson, and he died before the ship was finished. Completed, Vasa was 69 metres long and more than 50 metres from keel to masthead, and fitted out with ten sails, 64 cannon, 120 tonnes of ballast and hundreds of sculptures she weighed over 1,200 tonnes.

Before she sailed, her captain, Söfring Hansson, showed Vice Admiral Klas Fleming a worrying test. He had thirty men run back and forth across the deck, and the ship rolled so alarmingly that Fleming stopped the test for fear she would sink at the quay.1 Under pressure from the king, Fleming ordered her to sail anyway. On 10 August 1628, about 1,300 metres into her maiden voyage and still in sight of the shipyard, a gust heeled her to port and water poured in through the open gunports. Within minutes she lay on the bottom, 32 metres down. Roughly thirty people died.

The inquest punished no one. The officers claimed innocence; the builders said they had followed the design the king approved. Experts judged that the ship had too little belly, not enough hull to carry her heavy upper works, and the blame fell on Hybertsson, who was dead. Shipwrights of the day had no way to calculate stability in advance; that mathematics lay more than a century in the future. The yard's Swedish and Dutch workers also spoke different languages, trained in different traditions and used two different systems of measurement. It is hardly a surprise that the ship turned out to be asymmetrical.

Vasa stayed in the harbour mud. In the 1660s divers using a diving bell brought up almost all her guns. On 25 August 1956 a fuels engineer, Anders Franzén, pulled up a core of black, waterlogged oak off the island of Beckholmen, and on 24 April 1961 Vasa broke the surface after 333 years.

concepts.title: Mary Rose: A Veteran, Not a Maiden
concepts.contentHtml:
Here is a mix-up you will meet often: the Mary Rose sank on her maiden voyage, just like Vasa. She did not. Henry VIII's warship was built in Portsmouth from 1510 and served for 34 years, sailing as far as Scotland in the north and the Atlantic coast of France in the south.1 The Mary Rose Trust suggests how the myth arose: when the Mary Rose was raised, Vasa's 1961 salvage was the only comparable operation, so it featured in press releases, and the maiden-voyage story attached itself to the wrong ship.

She sank on 19 July 1545 in the Battle of the Solent, when some 200 French ships attempted to invade England, and Henry VIII watched from Southsea Castle. Of about 500 men aboard, only a few dozen survived. Why she went down is still argued, and the evidence pulls several ways:

  • Wind and gunports: the only confirmed eyewitness, a Flemish survivor, said she had fired her starboard guns and was turning when a gust heeled her over and water poured in through the open lowest gunports.
  • Command: it was Sir George Carew's first naval command, and the claim that he had men he could not rule comes from his own cousin, who may have been protecting the family name.
  • Overloading: she had more guns after a refit, but studies of her size and armament suggest she was still within safe limits, and she had crossed the Channel with them.
  • French guns: a French cavalry officer said French cannon sank her, but the granite ball found aboard was in her own shot locker, and that stone also occurs in England's West Country.

Notice how the Trust weighs each claim against its source: a cousin with a motive, a French officer whose side needed a victory, a stone that could have come from either country. Most accounts agree that she was turning when she heeled over; why the turn became a capsize is still debated. Volunteer divers found her timbers on 1 May 1971, and the hull was lifted in a steel cradle on 11 October 1982.

concepts.title: The Long Drying
concepts.contentHtml:
Raising a wreck is the easy part. Waterlogged wood can look sound, but bacteria have weakened its cells, and the water inside is now holding them up. Let it dry and the wood shrinks and cracks, because the surface tension of evaporating water can collapse the weakened cells. Both teams chose polyethylene glycol (PEG), a water-soluble synthetic wax also used in cosmetics, which soaks into the wood and takes the place of the water.

Vasa came first. Spraying began in April 1962, at first by hand: five men needed five hours to cover the ship. From 1965 an automatic system with 500 nozzles sprayed her inside and out, the PEG concentration rising from 10 percent to about 45 percent. The spray treatment lasted 17 years, from April 1962 to January 1979, and was followed by nine years of slow air-drying.1 Then came a shock. In the rainy summer of 2000, yellow and white spots appeared on the timbers: humidity was combining with sulphur in the wood to make destructive acids. A new climate system came on line in 2004, and over seven years the ship's 4,000 rusty iron bolts were replaced with corrosion-resistant steel. Vasa still settles about a millimetre a year, and in places her timber has lost 40 to 80 percent of its load-bearing strength, so a new support structure is being installed with the aim of finishing it by 2028, her 400th anniversary.

The Mary Rose followed Vasa's lead. From December 1982 she was sprayed with chilled, filtered fresh water to keep her wet and wash out salts. PEG spraying ran in two phases. Phase one, with a low-molecular-weight PEG, began on 30 September 1994 and ran until 2003; phase two, with a higher-molecular-weight PEG, ran from 2004 to 2013. Then a sealed hot box dried her at about 55 percent humidity and 20 °C, and more than 100 tonnes of water left the timbers between 2013 and 2016, 34 years after she was raised.

title: Into the Deep: Black Sea, Endurance, Titanic
description: Robots in the abyss: an intact Greek ship, Shackleton's Endurance, and the Titanic's slow vanishing

concepts.title: A Greek Ship Two Kilometres Down
concepts.contentHtml:
Between 2015 and 2017 the Black Sea Maritime Archaeology Project (Black Sea MAP), led by the University of Southampton with Bulgarian partners, surveyed more than 2,000 square kilometres of seabed off Bulgaria. Its main aim was environmental: to study how the region changed as sea level rose after the last glacial cycle. Along the way it found 65 shipwrecks, from Roman trading vessels complete with amphorae to a 17th-century Cossack raiding fleet. It also excavated an Early Bronze Age settlement at Ropotamo, whose house timbers and hearths now lie 2.5 metres below the seabed, abandoned as the water rose.

In late 2017 the team found the wreck that made headlines the next year: a Greek trading ship of a type previously seen only in paintings on ancient Greek pottery, such as the Siren Vase in the British Museum. The wreck lies more than two kilometres down, where oxygen-free conditions can preserve organic material for thousands of years. A small piece of the vessel was carbon dated, confirming that the ship is at least 2,400 years old, from around 400 BCE.1 That makes it the oldest intact shipwreck known. The project's principal investigator, Jon Adams, said that an intact Classical ship in over two kilometres of water was something he would never have believed possible.

How do you study a wreck two kilometres down without touching it? From the survey ship, the team flew two ROVs. One filmed the wrecks and photographed them for photogrammetry; the other carried high-definition cameras and lasers to map the seabed. By matching millions of points in overlapping images, the archaeologists built 3D models of each wreck as it lies, then draped the models with textures from the photographs. In the earlier seasons some wrecks had been found with their masts still upright.

The approach is a new kind of archaeology: survey first, record completely, and excavate only if there is a strong reason. For a wreck two kilometres down, a well-made model may be the only visit most scholars will ever make.

concepts.title: Endurance: The Finest Wooden Wreck
concepts.contentHtml:
You may know the story from the Exploration topic: Shackleton's Endurance was trapped and crushed by sea ice in the Weddell Sea and sank in November 1915. Her captain, Frank Worsley, had to fix the position on an overcast day without the sun, using earlier sextant readings and an estimate of how the ice was drifting. For a century, the Weddell Sea's thick, almost permanent ice made a search close to impossible.

In 2022 the Endurance22 expedition, mounted by the Falklands Maritime Heritage Trust aboard the South African icebreaker Agulhas II, sent Saab Sabertooth underwater vehicles to comb a search area it had defined before leaving Cape Town. Endurance was spotted in the Weddell Sea at a depth of 3,008 metres, about four miles south of Worsley's estimated position, on the 100th anniversary of Shackleton's funeral.1 Luck helped: that season saw the lowest extent of Antarctic sea ice recorded in the satellite era.

What the cameras showed astonished the team. The hull sits upright and intact, well proud of the seabed; the masts are down and the rigging is tangled, but the name ENDURANCE still arcs across the stern, with the five-pointed Polaris star beneath it. The marine archaeologist Mensun Bound called it by far the finest wooden shipwreck he had ever seen. Why so good? The deep-sea biologist Michelle Taylor saw little wood deterioration and inferred that the wood-munching animals found elsewhere in the ocean are absent from the forest-free Antarctic. Instead the wreck is sprinkled with filter feeders: stalked sea squirts, anemones, sponges, brittlestars and crinoids.

Nothing was brought up. Endurance is a designated Historic Site and Monument under the Antarctic Treaty and must not be disturbed in any way, so the team recorded it entirely in images. A wreck 107 years old and three kilometres down was studied in detail and left exactly where it lay.

concepts.title: Titanic: A Wreck Being Eaten
concepts.contentHtml:
On 1 September 1985 a joint American-French expedition led by Robert Ballard of the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and Jean-Louis Michel of the French research institute IFREMER found the Titanic, about 350 nautical miles off Newfoundland and some 3,800 metres down. It lies in two pieces. Unlike the wooden wrecks in this topic, it is a steel ship, and the deep is taking it apart in a different way.

The hull is draped in rusticles, icicle-like growths of rust. They look solid but are highly porous and host a complex community of bacteria. In 2010 researchers from Dalhousie University in Canada and the University of Seville described a new species, Halomonas titanicae, isolated from a rusticle that had been removed from the wreck in 1991; in tests it clung to steel and built knob-like mounds of corrosion. Salt corrosion and strong deep-ocean currents do the rest.

The losses are visible. In 2019 a team led by Victor Vescovo revisited the wreck for the first time in 14 years and found that it had degraded considerably, especially the officers' quarters on the starboard side. The Titanic historian Parks Stephenson said the captain's bathtub, a favourite image among enthusiasts, was gone. How long the rest will last is uncertain. Henrietta Mann, one of the scientists who described the bacterium, predicted that the microbes could devour the entire wreck by 2030, yet the bow and many interiors were still well preserved in 2019.1 Treat any date as a projection, not a fact.

The lesson of the Titanic is that cold and deep does not mean safe. What preserves a wreck is the absence of whatever attacks its material: borers for wood, corrosion and iron-loving microbes for steel. In 1986 the US Congress passed the R.M.S. Titanic Maritime Memorial Act, which calls for the site to be recognised as an international maritime memorial: the slowly vanishing wreck is also a grave.

title: Finders Keepers? Law, Ethics and the Dead
description: Treasure hunting against archaeology, the Mercedes case, the 2001 UNESCO Convention and war graves

concepts.title: Finders Keepers? The Mercedes Case
concepts.contentHtml:
Is a sunken treasure simply the finder's? On 5 October 1804 a squadron of Spanish frigates sailing home from Montevideo, only a day from Cádiz, was intercepted by four British warships under Commodore Graham Moore, sent to stop Spanish warships carrying treasure. In what became the Battle of Cape Saint Mary, the frigate Nuestra Señora de las Mercedes exploded only a few minutes after the fighting began. Except for about fifty sailors, everyone aboard was killed, among them the wife and seven children of Captain Alvear, who had moved to another ship of the squadron.

In 2007 the American company Odyssey Marine Exploration found a wreck site in international waters west of the Strait of Gibraltar, 1,100 metres deep and scattered over an area 368 by 110 metres. Odyssey recovered approximately 594,000 coins and a number of other small artefacts,1 flew them to Tampa in Florida, and asked a US court to grant it the treasure under the law of finds (ownership of abandoned property) or, failing that, a reward under the law of salvage. Spain replied that the wreck was the Mercedes, a Spanish navy frigate, and that as a sunken warship it was protected by sovereign immunity under the US Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act. Peru and 25 individuals, most claiming descent from people with cargo aboard, made claims of their own.

In September 2011 the US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit agreed with Spain. The evidence identified the wreck as the Mercedes, and the immunity covered the whole wreck, cargo included, even if some of the cargo had belonged to private people. Odyssey's argument that the frigate had been on a commercial voyage did not persuade the court. In February 2012 the coins arrived in Spain, and an emergency appeal by Peru, which argued that the silver had been mined and minted on its soil, was turned down.

So the popular idea of finders keepers fails at the first test. A sunken warship remains the property of its government, however long it has lain on the seabed, and nobody may salvage it without that government's permission.

concepts.title: The 2001 Convention: Leave It Where It Lies?
concepts.contentHtml:
The Mercedes case was decided under US law. The international standard is UNESCO's Convention on the Protection of the Underwater Cultural Heritage, adopted on 2 November 2001 and in force since 2 January 2009. It covers all traces of human existence of a cultural, historical or archaeological character that have been under water for at least 100 years. Two of its principles cut directly against treasure hunting:

  • In situ first: preservation where the heritage lies is to be considered as the first option before any activity directed at it.1
  • No commercial exploitation: underwater cultural heritage is not to be traded, sold, bought or bartered as commercial goods.

Why does sale worry archaeologists so much? The Belitung wreck, a 9th-century ship found off Indonesia, is the classic case. A salvage firm, Seabed Explorations, recovered some 60,000 artefacts in 1998 and 1999, including Tang-dynasty Chinese ceramics and gold, and in 2005 a corporation set up by Singapore's government bought the cargo for US$32 million. Archaeologists argued that a commercial salvor has every incentive to chase eye-catching treasure rather than humble potsherds, and the maritime archaeologist Filipe Castro said such excavation silences all the questions the vessel could have answered. The firm's head, Tilman Walterfang, replied that without his company there would be no data on the wreck at all; the company acknowledged that a good portion of the artefacts were raised without precise documentation, blaming looting threats and government demands for haste.

Both sides have a point worth weighing. Looters had begun circling the Belitung site after fishermen found it, so leaving a wreck in place protects it only if someone polices it. And the Convention binds only states that join it: Indonesia, Singapore and the United States were not parties in 2017, and in 2016 the marine archaeologist Innes McCartney noted that the UK had not ratified it either, out of concern that it would be too difficult or expensive to enforce.

concepts.title: War Graves and Vanishing Wrecks
concepts.contentHtml:
Some wrecks are graves, and that changes the ethics again. In February and March 1942, during the Java Sea campaign, Japanese forces sank Dutch, British and American warships, and many of their crews went down with them. Amateur divers found the Dutch wrecks almost intact in 2002. In November 2016 a survey sponsored by the Karel Doorman Fund, which represents the crews' next of kin, reported that the wrecks of two Dutch warships, HNLMS De Ruyter and HNLMS Java, appeared to be missing, and that a large part of a third, the Kortenaer, had gone too. Sonar showed only their imprints in the seabed. Two British wrecks, HMS Exeter and HMS Encounter, had been almost entirely scavenged for scrap, and the US submarine Perch had vanished.

The likely culprits were illegal metal salvagers, encouraged by what McCartney called a perfect storm of high metal prices and weak enforcement. For the families, the loss was not about artefacts: the fund's president, Jacques Brandt, said they considered the ships war graves that should never be tampered with. For archaeology, McCartney said, the Battle of the Java Sea could now never be studied on the seabed.

The law lags behind. The Commonwealth War Graves Commission said the Java Sea wrecks had never been formally designated as war graves. In the United Kingdom only 67 ship wrecks, plus all military aircraft lost under water, are protected places under the Protection of Military Remains Act 1986,1 and outside the UK the Act can in practice only be enforced against British citizens, British-flagged ships or vessels landing in the UK.

Meanwhile science keeps asking to study the dead. DNA from Vasa's skeletons showed in 2023 that one person long thought to be a man was a woman, and the Antikythera bones may yet reveal who sailed with the mechanism. Studying the dead and respecting them are both duties. Every wreck with human remains, from a Tudor warship to a cruiser in the Java Sea, forces a choice about how to balance them.
